title: An Experimental Scheme for Testing Molecular Rectification with Only Micrometer-Scale Fabrication Requirements
abstract: In our previous work, we proposed a theoretical model capable of inducing sustained directed transport without consuming information or external energy. However, the experimental verification schemes proposed previously were technically challenging, and the model has therefore not yet been experimentally tested. In this work, we propose a greatly simplified experimental design. By introducing hydrophilic functional groups onto the tip of a gold needle through surface modification and pressing the needle against one of two liquid-vapor interfaces, the compressed interface is maintained at a higher ionic concentration than the other interface, thereby sustaining a concentration difference between them. This design reduces the fabrication requirement from the nanometer scale to the micrometer scale, substantially lowering experimental complexity and facilitating experimental examination of the proposed mechanism.
summary: This work proposes a significantly simplified experimental setup to test a theory of molecular rectification—the directed flow of molecules without external energy. By using a hydrophilic needle on a porous membrane, the authors can create and maintain an ionic concentration gradient at micrometer scales. This greatly lowers the technical barrier for experimentally validating this non-equilibrium transport mechanism.
main_problem: The paper addresses the experimental verification of a theoretical model predicting sustained directed transport (molecular rectification) without external energy input.
main_result: A simplified, micrometer-scale experimental design is proposed that can sustain a measurable concentration difference and confirm the predicted directed flow cycle by observing steady liquid levels or pressure differences.
method: The authors combine theoretical derivations based on chemical potential, Laplace's equation, and osmotic equilibrium with proposals for novel, low-complexity microfluidic/interfacial experiments.
model_or_system: The system involves a hydrophobic porous membrane separating two liquid-vapor interfaces. Directed transport is driven by maintaining an ionic concentration gradient ($	ext{C}_a - 	ext{C}_b$) using a hydrophilic needle tip to locally modify the interface, analogous to semipermeable membranes.
key_observables: Sustained directed flow (steady state), measurable pressure differences ($P_n$ and $P_d$), and liquid-level differences ($	ext{A}_1$ vs $	ext{B}_1$).
important_parameters: Fabrication scale reduced to micrometer level; theoretical maximum pressures up to 288,000 Pa for water.
main_assumptions: Assumes the charged groups act like a semipermeable membrane and employs ideal dilute solution approximations ($\pi = CRT$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup using a porous membrane and needle tip (Fig. 1, Fig. 3), showing interface deformation and ion release. Supplementary figures detail MD simulations of directed flux ($	ext{NNWM}$) and alternative experimental configurations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical basis for rectification via concentration gradients to proposing a simplified, low-complexity experimental platform using micrometer fabrication requirements, supported by both analytical derivations and simulation results.
why_interesting: While focused on classical thermodynamics and transport, the underlying principles of non-equilibrium steady states driven by interfacial energy minimization are highly relevant to open quantum systems modeling, particularly those involving dissipation or boundary effects.
